chapter_theme: Pattinathar's Thiruthillai, twenty venbas to the Lord of the hall at Chidambaram. The living are corpses who weep over the dead; kings burn to a fistful of ash; the wealth and theatres of rulers vanish when the Lord's mind turns. Against this the poet asks for a different wealth, the one that comes with not killing, not lying, not being angry and not being refused by the asker, names the Lord as the one who makes all eat, sleep, embrace and dance on the rope of deeds, and finds in remembering the feet and chanting the five letters the medicine against dying and the way out of birth. The Lord's own entourage of bull, serpent and ghouls, his begging in a skull and his dance seen only after aeons of tapas close the picture.
structure_note: 283, 284 and 285 share the refrain செல்வந் தருவாய், சிதம்பர தேசிகனே and are lists of abstentions in -ஆமல். 290 and 293 are catalogues of what the Lord makes happen (-விப்பான், -பான்). 289 alone is addressed to the goddess Sivakama Sundari; 288, 295 and 296 to the poet's own mind or heart. The rest address the Lord of the hall under different names (சங்கரன், அம்பலவாணர், சிதம்பர தேசிகன், ஆனந்தத் தாண்டவன்).

280.reading: Having left the many desires that cling to women with broad shoulders like bamboo, to gold and to land, and died, the corpse that goes: the corpses that will die later gather round it in a crowd, roll on the ground and cry. What, asks the poet, is he to do?
280.nuance: போம்பிணம் and சாம்பிணம், the corpse that goes and the corpses that will die, make the mourners already corpses; the dead man's one act was to leave his desires, which the mourners have not.

281.reading: The land gives rice and the rubbish heap gives cloth; when the poet sees the devotees his hands rise and his evil deeds descend; and whenever he sees the dance of the ash-smeared Lord of the little hall, his eyes well, his heart melts, and so does his inner self.
281.nuance: The first line is the renouncer's economy: food from any country, clothing from what is thrown away. The stanza is the one place in the chapter where the poet speaks of what he has rather than what he lacks, and the dance is its object.

282.reading: Instead of melting like butter in fire and doing austerity standing in the shade of the Lord of the golden hall, the poet took garlands fitted to the hair of cruel women, did them menial service, and poured pearls from a sieve to water worthless grass: such was his fate.
282.nuance: விழலுக்கு முத்து இறைத்தல், irrigating vizhal grass with pearls, is a stock figure for waste; here the pearls are his years of service. விதிவசம் puts the waste down to fate, as 260 did, which the chapter's later stanzas on the Lord as sole agent complicate.

283.reading: Without running off, without toiling for waste, without joining those who speak with partiality, without leaving the company of the good, without harbouring hot anger in the heart, without slipping from what is good, without seeking and putting off to today and tomorrow: give me wealth, teacher of Chidambaram.
283.nuance: The wealth asked for in 283 to 285 is tradition's riddle: either literal wealth that costs none of these faults, or the abstentions themselves as the only wealth. The last clause, இன்றைக்கு நாளைக்கென்று தேடாமல், not hunting day to day, tells against the literal reading.

284.reading: Without saying 'there is nothing' to those who ask, without even looking; without sins drawing near through speaking of faults; without the mind fainting and straying; without leaving service undone; without joining those who have not won love: give me wealth, teacher of Chidambaram.
284.nuance: The first abstention is the sharpest: refusing an asker without so much as looking at him (பாராமல்). The poet, himself a mendicant, asks for wealth on condition that it never be concealed from askers.

285.reading: Without killing, without eating what was killed, without learning deceit and seizing, without consorting with tricksters, without lying even in a dream, without listening to idle words, without going into the maya of women: give me wealth, teacher of Chidambaram.
285.nuance: Killing and eating the killed head the list, as they do in the poet's confession at 276. கனவினும் பொய் சொல்லாமல் uses the Kural's test of a settled nature.

286.reading: Crowned kings and all the rest are in the end burnt to a fistful of ash and become earth; even having seen this, people think of nothing but this grasping life, and no one knows that to be saved we must reach the feet of the Lord of the golden hall.
286.nuance: கண்டு பின்னும், having seen and still: the reproach is not ignorance of death but the failure to let what is seen change anything. பிடிசார்ந்த வாழ்வு, the life one holds in a fist, answers பிடிசாம்பர், the fistful of ash.

287.reading: The morning's condition is excrement and urine; besides that, at high noon the heavy condition is hunger and thirst, and the accumulated deeds; the evening's condition is sleep and lust. Remove these, Lord of the hall who wears the poison, and take me as yours.
287.nuance: உபாதி, the limiting adjunct of Siddhanta, is applied to the body's daily needs by the three times of day. சஞ்சிதம், the store of past karma, sits oddly between hunger and sleep; it may be a fourth condition or may qualify noon's hunger as the fruit of past deeds. ஆலமுகந்தருள் is read as 'who took the poison' (ஆலம் உகந்து).

288.reading: If you go near the Lord of the hall of famed Tillai, the bull charges and the serpent bites; if you follow behind him, ghosts, his troops and the big-headed bhutas follow you. Where will you go, mind? To the place where the dwellers of the corpse-forest go.
288.nuance: The Lord is approached through his terrifying retinue, and the last line is a wry answer: the mind's only destination is the cremation ground, which is where the Lord himself dwells and dances. பிணக்காடவர் may be the Lord as dweller of the corpse-forest or the dead who are taken there; the two readings converge.

289.reading: He takes a skull, wraps a hide about him, strolls slowly from house to house collecting alms like a man without a destiny, and with a maddening grace stands here in the hall: what, the poet asks Sivakama Sundari, is the reckoning in seeking out this mendicant?
289.nuance: Siva as Bhikshatana, the begging ascetic, is described to his consort with the irony of a complaint: what can be gained from a god who begs? ஆடுமருள், dancing or maddening grace, and கணக்கு, account, carry the sense; the stanza may also be the poet's self-mockery for seeking such a god. It is the only stanza addressed to the goddess.

290.reading: The one who makes us eat and makes us sleep, who sets one thing against another and makes us embrace, who shows the deeds we have done, and who makes us dance along the bond-rope of the two deeds: there is such a one in the hall of Tillai.
290.nuance: Eight causatives in -விப்பான் make the Lord the agent of everything from eating to quarrelling; the puppet of 240 is here the doctrine of a single mover. The rope is இருவினைப் பாசக் கயிறு, the two deeds as the bond, so the Lord works through karma rather than apart from it.

291.reading: If one bows at the feet of the Lord of the hall who is easy for his devotees, one may win the boon of a wealth that does not die; we are those who see the family of the grace of the eternal, stainless one whom the tall one who measured the seven worlds and Brahma could not see, and he is our clan deity.
291.nuance: மடியாமற் செல்வம், wealth that does not die, is the wealth 283 to 285 asked for. குலதெய்வம், the family god, and அருட்குடி, the household of grace, turn the clan vocabulary the Siddhars attack into the devotees' own kinship.

292.reading: Divine Lord of Chidambaram, if your mind turns away, where is the dream-like life of kings built on lies, where the earth, where the wealth called real, where the platforms of the provincial lords, where the theatre halls they set up with their hands? All of it is a bewilderment of the eye.
292.nuance: The condition is the Lord's will (உன் சித்தம் திரும்பிவிட்டால்), so the stanza makes royal splendour depend moment by moment on him. நாடகசாலை, the theatre, is the Kural's image for wealth's crowd (332). கண்மயக்கு closes as விழிமயக்கு closed 253.

293.reading: The one who clothes and the one who feeds milk-rice, the one who saves a man and the one who ruins him, the one who asks 'what is this?', the one who gives so that the goal is reached, the one who begs saying 'give', and the one who stands and prevents the giving: are you not all of these, dancer of bliss of Tillai?
293.nuance: The Lord is both the beggar and the one who stops the gift, both saviour and destroyer; the stanza refuses to leave him on one side of any transaction. It extends 290 from the bodily life to giving and refusing, the chapter's own concern.

294.reading: Though one talks grandly, climbs on stilts, chants 'thaththaara' and dances the pavuri, though one speaks of one's elder brother's or younger brother's ambition, does anything come of it? Apart from the word of the Maker who fills Tillai there are no deeds.
294.nuance: சோங்கு is taken as stilts and பவுரி as a whirling dance; தம்முன் தம்பி அத்தாசை is obscure, perhaps the ambitions of brothers for one another. The point of the catalogue is display without result; கன்மங்கள், deeds, exist only as the Maker's (கத்தா) word, which makes 290 explicit.

295.reading: One must win the boon of not being born; and having been born, there is a medicine for not dying, see how it is: heart, do not forget the lotus feet of the Lord of the dharma-rich hall of Tillai; see, that is the good medicine for you.
295.nuance: இறவாதிருக்க மருந்து, a medicine against dying, is the Siddhars' promise, usually kept by breath or kalpa herbs; Pattinathar names remembrance of the feet as the drug. Whether the deathlessness is bodily or the end of rebirth is not said.

296.reading: Do not despair, heart: if you chant without flagging, by the five letters, the Sankara who dwells in Tillai, the mine of knowledge who fills the earth, the destroyer of the cities, the lamp that does not go out, the dancer in the golden hall, the release that is not being born again will be attained.
296.nuance: செவியாமல் in line 4 is read as சலியாமல், without wearying, since the sense needs a manner of chanting; பிறவா முத்தி, release as not being born, defines the goal negatively. The stanza follows 295's medicine with the method.

297.reading: Those who trust the Lord of the hall, who is the meaning of the four Vedas, yet stay without once going to serve him: they are made to lift black stones onto their heads, their hands are nailed into fetters, they are set again on one leg, and his servants come and bind them.
297.nuance: The syntax is strained: நம்பியவர் and சேவிக்கொணாதிருப்பார் may be one group (those who trust but do not serve) or two, and the torments of lines 3 and 4 read as Yama's punishments for failing to serve, with the agents left unnamed. கிட்டியும் may be a crushing device. The reading is the sense most editors give it.

298.reading: Those who do not praise the Lord of the hall who dances adorned with the river and the thumbai flower have a sign on this earth: no food, no comfort, no kin, no cloth, and even if they beg, no alms, so that they stay pining.
298.nuance: Poverty is read as the visible mark (அடையாளம்) of not praising the Lord, a karmic claim the chapter does not make elsewhere; 281, where the renouncer eats from any land and clothes himself from the rubbish heap, is its counterweight.

299.reading: To see the Father, the overlord of the thirty-three crore gods, the eternal one, the lover of the mother Sivakama Sundari, our dancer, the lord who dances in the golden hall, how many crores of ages have these eyes been doing tapas!
299.nuance: The eyes, not the poet, are the ascetics: seeing the dance is the fruit of aeons. The stanza closes the work on the sight that 281 said melts him.

links.note: The Naladiyar ends its funeral-drum stanza with சாவார் சாப்பிணம் சுமப்பார், the dying carry the dead; Pattinathar's mourners are சாம்பிணம், corpses that will die, rolling and crying round the corpse that has gone. Both make the funeral a procession of corpses; Pattinathar adds that the dead man at least left his desires.

Tirumular says the quality that comes to those who have seen the holy dance in the hall comes to those who hear of it too, and compares it to drink; Pattinathar says that whenever he sees the dance of the Lord of the little hall his eyes well and his heart and inner self melt. Both describe the dance as an intoxication of the seer.

The Kural defines virtue as what proceeds without envy, craving, anger and harsh speech; Pattinathar's 'wealth' is a life without partiality, hot anger, slipping from good or daily seeking. Both define the good by what it abstains from, and both place anger in the heart (நெஞ்சில் / உள்ளத்து) rather than in act.

The Kural asks where the life of the one who conceals hides when the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal; Pattinathar asks for a wealth that never says 'there is nothing' to askers without even looking at them. Both treat refusal of the asker as a kind of killing.

The Kural says the standing of life lies in not eating flesh and that hell does not open its mouth for the eater; Pattinathar heads his conditions for wealth with not killing and not eating what was killed. Both put killing and eating together and before the other faults.

The Naladiyar says even kings on elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and no one is left; Pattinathar says crowned kings and all the rest burn to a fistful of ash, and that even seeing it people cling to life. The Naladiyar's lesson is impermanence; Pattinathar's is that seeing it does not teach.

Sivavakkiyar says people have seen the body lying there and the life slipped out, and still do not take it in; Pattinathar says people have seen kings burnt to ash and still think only of this grasping life. Both separate seeing death (காண்) from realising it.

Both name the same three bodily needs, food, sleep and pleasure: Sivavakkiyar uses them to level caste (they are alike for you and me), Pattinathar names them as the day's three conditions (உபாதி) and asks the Lord to remove them. The same facts serve an argument about birth in one and about release in the other.

Sivavakkiyar asks what the life of Namban is, dancing surrounded by dogs in the loveless forest where ghouls eat corpses; Pattinathar tells his mind that near the Lord the bull charges, the serpent bites and ghosts and bhutas follow, and that its only destination is where the dwellers of the corpse-forest go. Both approach the Lord through the cremation ground and its company.

In 240 the poet is a string puppet who cannot move if the cord that is the Lord fails; in 290 the Lord is named as the one who makes all beings eat, sleep, embrace and dance on the rope of the two deeds. The personal confession becomes a doctrine of a single mover working through karma.

The Kural says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance hall and goes like that crowd breaking up; Pattinathar asks where the kings' wealth and their hand-built theatre halls (நாடகசாலை) are once the Lord's mind turns. Both use the theatre for the vanishing of wealth; Pattinathar makes the Lord the one who empties it.

On the reading of 273 in which 'all is Siva's doing' is the poet's own conclusion, 294 states it outright: apart from the Maker's word there are no deeds, and grand talk, stilts and dancing achieve nothing. On the other reading of 273, where the line is the learned men's excuse, 294 supplies the doctrine they misuse.

Arunagirinathar calls Thiruttani the physician of the disease of birth and asks to cut birth's root; Pattinathar says there is a medicine against dying for one already born, and that it is remembering the Lord's feet. Both borrow the Siddhars' medical language for devotion rather than for herbs or breath.

Tirumular says that when the inner maya and the three impurities go and one chants சிவாய, those letters end karma that is hard to remove; Pattinathar says chanting the Lord by the five letters without flagging brings the release that is not being born again. Both make the five letters the means and the end of birth the result.

source_issues: 296 line 4 has a stray character, நீ£செபித்தாற், for நீ செபித்தாற்; and செவியாமல் in the same line cannot be construed as it stands (read as சலியாமல்).
287 line 1 காலையுபாதி and line 3 மாலையுபாதி are printed as single words; the stanza's ஆலமுகந்தரு ளம்பலவா is spaced across the word boundary.
297 lines 2 to 4 have no clear subject for the torments described; the text may have lost a word (see the verse's nuance).
